posts.title: 7 Places to find Blessed McGivney
posts.description: Blessed Michael McGivney (1852–1890), founder of the Knights of Columbus, was a humble American priest whose vision of charity, fraternity, and faith transformed countless lives. Born to Irish immigrant parents in Connecticut, he overcame poverty, personal loss, and numerous obstacles to realize his priestly vocation. Though he died at just 38, he lived a remarkable life. From his birthplace to the seminaries where he studied and the parishes where he served, these seven sites retrace his journey. 1. Waterbury, Connecticut (1852–1868): His birthplace and first Mass Blessed Michael McGivney was born in Waterbury on August 12, 1852, to Irish immigrant parents. Raised in modest circumstances, he worked in a brass factory before pursuing the priesthood. At Immaculate Conception Church, he received his first sacraments and, following his ordination in 1877, returned to celebrate his first Mass. posts.title: Leo, last minute, and unusual: The Advent devotional to buy today
posts.description: When we think of interactive books, we generally envision children arranging pop-up castles or turning pages. But this unique Advent devotional is not a kid’s book. And it’s available in English or Spanish with one click, so if you’ve put off making an Advent plan until these last few hours, Lift Up Your Eyes: Advent with Pope Leo XIV is for you. Basically this is an Advent guided prayer journal, but the journal is on your computer or smartphone, and stays there. Each day’s reflection and prayer provide you with thought-provoking questions, and you can jot down your thoughts, no pen or paper required. But don’t worry, you don’t need an app or a subscription, and: Your notes stay with you. Your notes and settings are saved only in this browser, on this device. posts.title: Why are we so fascinated by what the pope wears?
posts.description: When Pope Leo appeared in a beautiful sky-blue chasuble during his recent visit to Argentina, he certainly caught people’s attention. And quite rightly, too. It was a stunning shade of blue, and not exactly what we’re accustomed to seeing at Mass. But the Holy Father wasn’t experimenting with a new look. His choice of vestments for Mass at the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján on November 11 had a special significance. Blue, which isn’t ordinarily a permitted liturgical color, is allowed in certain places through a special privilege associated with devotion to the Immaculate Conception. And the Pope’s chasuble echoed the blue mantle of Our Lady of Luján, Argentina’s beloved patroness. In other words, his wardrobe was telling a story. Catholic vestments can be extraordinary things. From delicate hand-embroidered flowers to elaborate gold thread, intricate crosses and beautifully woven fabrics, some are genuine works of art.
